bad.1: Doesn't say who makes the final call. The owner takes the assistant as the gatekeeper ('3 approved, 7 rejected, I only need to look at 2'), and when a bad expense gets paid he blames the tool.
bad.2: '(3rd submission)' is internal shorthand (and 'good-3' / 'quiet-5' are internal IDs). The owner can't tell what it means, so he never opens these two.
bad.4: Raw values (a cost-centre code, a project tag, a link) put in front of the person deciding, with no word on what each one is or what making them requirements would do. He can't tell, so he doesn't dare decide.
bad.5: The empty home only says 'select a course' while every number below is 0. A new instructor doesn't know why it's all zero or what to do next.
bad.6: The owner can't tell who 'employees who haven't submitted yet' covers (it is also the only button without a count), so he never clicks it.
bad.7: Can't tell these are counts, or counts of what (reports? dollars? people?), and the order runs backwards: reimbursed comes after submitted.
bad.8: 'Automatically sends' is read as 'all of these go out on their own', so nobody clicks the per-group explanation buttons. It never says which message is automatic and which still needs his click.
bad.10: It is the student's turn, but 'Waiting 1 hour' reads as 'the student has been waiting on me for an hour'.
bad.11: The owner reads 'results not guaranteed' and shrugs: it's boilerplate. It never names the real consequence (a pointless purchase can be paid automatically), which also clashes with wanting every expense to have a real business reason.
bad.12: The 'Suggested' rewrite is a first-person fill-in-the-blank about an experience. A student who never baked the loaf fills in the blanks and hands in a bake that never happened.
bad.13: No filter is set, yet it tells him to adjust his filters.
bad.15: The risk sits in three lines of small print, and the button only says 'I understand, turn on'. The owner clicked without reading them.
bad.16: The tab is called 'Blocked' but everything inside says 'Ban'. He can't tell whether blocking and banning are the same thing.
bad.17: 'The 3 angles in the brief': the instructor doesn't know which three are meant, and clicks 'All must follow an angle' anyway.
bad.18: 'Snapshot history' and 'building the curve' are implementation words. The seller can't tell what is missing or what refreshing does.
bad.20: 'v2 · 1 open' is unreadable: version 2 of what, and one open what?
bad.21: The group is called 'Suggest sending back', but the suggested action is 'ask her to add it, which is not a send-back'. He can't tell what the button will do.
bad.22: Sends the work back for a preference the brief never asked for. The student asks 'is this a new rule?' and feels accused.
bad.23: Can't tell what 'featured' is based on: featured by whom, and how?
bad.25: Unreadable: 'install' and 'writes' are implementation words, and nobody knows what the short code is.
bad.26: The announcement carries no content; nobody can tell what changed.

good.3: The doubt is written on the button itself, so the owner decides knowing about it.
good.9: Explains the version clash plainly; the owner understood which clicks counted and which didn't.
good.14: Says who decides; after this line, owners stopped treating the assistant as the gatekeeper.
good.19: Dated, says the rule is new and not the student's fault, and points at what already meets it; the student didn't feel blamed and made the change.
good.24: Refuses and gives the reason; no misunderstanding followed.
good.27: The owner understood the report was already sent back and won't be paid unless he approves it.
